title: The Price of a Meal
heading: Dinners for Six Persons.—September.
policy: A recommended dinner and estimated prices printed in the book, not a household bill or a record of actual consumption. Catalogue date 1899; preface dated November 1888. No exact market-price year is established. The eleven priced entries below follow the English menu. They are priced lines, not a claim about the number or order of courses served.
calculation: 1s. = 12d.; £1 = 20s. = 240d. The eleven menu amounts sum to 317d., which equals £1 6s. 5d. Shares are each line’s pence divided by 317, rounded to one decimal place. The per-person mean is 317 ÷ 6 = 52.8333…d., displayed as about 52.83d.; this is arithmetic, not an observed portion price or a historically quoted decimal amount. Rounded shares may not sum to exactly 100%.
verification: Menu No. 2, p. 1412, section 3157, was checked against the scan. Rumpsteak and mushrooms share a single bracketed 5s. 6d. price: the combined amount is counted once. The wild duck’s pence digit is ink-obscured; zero is restored from the visible 4s. and reconciliation with the printed total. The Maitre d’Hotel sauce line supplies recipe no. 731 and 1s. but no independent quantity. All other row quantities and recipe numbers are transcribed below. Abbreviations are expanded in the display. Recipe 2006 is titled Liqueur Jelly, and names Maraschino as an option: it is the menu’s numbered reference, not a separate recipe titled Maraschino Jelly.

rows.name: Celery Soup
rows.note: The menu prices 2½ pints at 1s. 3d. Recipe 299 on p. 149 separately quotes 9d. per quart. These figures do not reconcile by simple volume scaling; the menu estimate is retained separately from the recipe’s price.
rows.method: Recipe 299 requires cutting celery, boiling, passing it through a sieve, adding stock, simmering, and finishing with cream or milk. It states one hour, but gives no separate allocation of active work, fuel or cleaning.
rows.equipment: A sieve is explicitly named. A cooking vessel is implied by boiling and simmering; no specific material or equipment purchase is required by the wording.

rows.name: Turbot with Cream Sauce
rows.note: The menu’s numbered recipe starts with remains of cold turbot. It tells the cook to remove skin and bone when the fish comes from table to reduce waste. The 3s. 6d. menu estimate does not explain how the previously cooked fish is valued.
rows.method: Recipe 576, p. 270, calls for trimming and cutting the cooked fish, melting butter in a stewpan, briefly simmering the sauce and warming the fish. Its stated ten minutes does not include catching, buying, originally cooking or storing the fish.
rows.equipment: A stewpan is explicitly named. The recipe does not establish ownership of a copper vessel, a refrigerator, or any specific fuel system.

rows.name: Chicken Croquettes
rows.note: The menu supplies six croquettes, recipe no. 1354, and an average cost of 1s. 6d. Method, ingredients and equipment have not been checked in this research pass; no preparation-time claim is made.

rows.name: Sweetbreads
rows.note: The menu lists sweetbreads separately from their Maitre d’Hotel sauce. The two prices are kept as separate entries. Method and portion size have not been verified here.

rows.name: Maître d’Hôtel Sauce
rows.note: The printed sauce line has recipe no. 731 and a 1s. price but no independent quantity. The sauce has its own stated price; its volume is unspecified.

rows.name: Rumpsteak and Mushrooms
rows.note: A printed brace groups the steak and mushrooms under one price. At 66d., this is the largest priced entry, about 20.8% of the total. The source gives a combined price for meat and mushrooms.

rows.name: Wild Duck
rows.note: The pence digit is ink-obscured. Zero is an editorial restoration consistent with the visible 4s. and the printed total after summing the other entries. This uncertainty is retained rather than presented as a perfectly clear reading.

rows.name: Valentia Pudding
rows.note: The menu names one pudding at 2s. 6d. A six-person dinner heading does not establish equal pudding portions; method and yield have not been checked here.

rows.name: Maraschino Jelly
rows.note: The referenced recipe is Liqueur Jelly, no. 2006, p. 938. Its method names Maraschino among suitable liqueurs. The recipe’s 2s. 6d. average cost with best gelatine matches this menu line; its stated yield is a quart mould.
rows.method: Recipe 2006 requires heating and skimming syrup and gelatine, straining lemon juice, filtering the jelly through a bag, setting a mould in ice, and unmoulding. Its ten-minute time line applies only to boiling the sugar and water, not making and setting the whole jelly.
rows.equipment: A saucepan, filtering bag and mould are explicitly named, and the method calls for ice. The quoted copper moulds elsewhere are examples from an equipment list, not proof that copper was necessary or used for this dinner.

rows.name: Macaroni Cheese
rows.note: The menu supplies one dish and a 1s. estimate. No precise serving weight, ingredient quantity or labour duration is established in this pass.

rows.name: Potatoes
rows.note: Potatoes are the smallest priced entry: 2d. for 2 lbs., about 0.6% of the dinner estimate. This is the cost assigned to the menu item, not evidence that preparation and fuel were free.

equipment.name: Two copper jelly moulds
equipment.note: Specification No. II, headed ‘Suitable for Good Class Houses.’ The amount is for two moulds together, not one. It is a supplier-based purchase quotation, not a cost incurred each time jelly is made.

equipment.name: Jelly bag and stand
equipment.note: Specification No. II, continued. The liqueur-jelly method names a bag but does not require this particular stand or prove that it was purchased. This quotation is separate from the meal estimate.

equipmentContext: On p. 89 the book says the utensil specifications are drawn from the catalogue of Messrs. Adams and Son, furnishing ironmongers, and offers a 10 per cent cash discount. The displayed quotations are the printed list prices before that discount. The specifications divide households by means and size; their class labels are the manual’s language, not classifications assigned by this exhibition. These are illustrative reusable purchases, not a minimum kitchen budget or the actual possessions of the dinner’s consumers.

missingCosts.title: Fuel and heat
missingCosts.text: The menu has no separate fuel line. Cooking methods require heat, but the stove, fuel, consumption and price for this dinner are unknown. No fuel surcharge has been invented.

missingCosts.title: Work and service
missingCosts.text: Wages, preparation, serving and cleaning are not separately itemised in the dinner table. The source does not define a complete accounting boundary, so absence of an itemised charge is not proof it was excluded from every estimate.

missingCosts.title: Cooling and storage
missingCosts.text: The jelly method calls for ice and the turbot starts with cooked remains. The menu provides no separate ice or storage charge and no equipment inventory for the hypothetical household.

missingCosts.title: Earlier preparation
missingCosts.text: Stock and already cooked fish carry prior inputs. The printed menu does not tell us how those inputs were allocated between meals. A recipe’s finishing time cannot recover their complete cost.

missingCosts.title: The occasion beyond the listed food
missingCosts.text: No separate wine service, table linen, lighting or room costs are listed. The menu does not establish which were supplied, how they were paid for, or whether this was an observed dinner party.

sourceNotes: Dinner: printed p. 1412, section 3157, menu No. 2; PDF sequence p. 1522; Archive page-number index leaf 1526. The local scan supplies the exact printed evidence.
Equipment context: p. 89, paragraphs 185–186; supplier attribution, household-size distinctions, and cash-discount condition checked visually.
Equipment list: p. 90, Specification II, two copper jelly moulds £1 1s.; p. 91, Specification II continued, jelly bag and stand 10s. 6d., checked visually.

Method checks: p. 149, recipe 299; p. 270, recipe 576; p. 938, recipe 2006. Method summaries are modern paraphrases, not complete transcriptions. The other eight priced entries have menu-level verification only.

Currency notation follows the Bank of England’s education resource: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/education/education-resources/shillings-to-pounds-converter . No modern purchasing-power equivalent is calculated.
No consumer’s class, income or actual spending is established. The existing p. 7 wage/staffing record is contextual only; no affordability percentage or wage-hours figure is calculated.
